question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: I would say I am a real team player and I get on with everyone. For me communication is the most important thing in any team, along with respect, honesty and a positive attitude. Conflict has never been a problem for me because I stay calm and professional whatever happens. Anyone who has worked with me would tell you that I am reliable, friendly and easy to work with, and I think those are the qualities that stop conflicts from starting in the first place.
reason: General statements and a list of qualities with no specific situation and no action of their own, so level 1.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: The one that comes to mind was at a parcel depot where I worked nights. There were two shift leads, one on inbound and one on outbound, and they had never really got on. It came to a head in the run-up to Christmas when the outbound lead started parking empty cages in the inbound lanes because he had run out of room. The inbound lead moved them back without saying anything, and this went on for about a week, with each of them getting more wound up. One night they had a proper shouting match in front of the whole shift by the loading doors. I was over on the far side of the building at the time, so I only heard about most of it afterwards. The depot manager came in early the next day, took them both into the office and was in there for over an hour. After that he had yellow lines painted to mark a cage park at the end of bay six, and he told the two of them to do a walk round together at the start of every shift. To be fair to him it worked, because the cages stopped turning up in the lanes and the two leads were at least civil to each other from then on. So that is how the conflict got resolved in our team.
reason: A specific conflict, but only what the two shift leads and the manager did; no action of the candidate's own, so level 1.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: Working with others to reach a shared goal is something I think every workplace depends on. In my view a good team is one where everybody knows their job, pulls their weight and trusts the people around them. If there were a disagreement I would want it talked through sensibly, and if someone were struggling I would expect the team to rally round, because that is how targets get met. Where I have seen teams go wrong it is usually down to poor leadership or people not listening to each other. I have always believed that if you treat people the way you want to be treated, the results follow, and that is the approach I would bring here.
reason: General statements and hypotheticals about how teams should work; no specific situation and no action of their own, so level 1.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: Last spring our team of four was asked to replace the booking engine for a chain of leisure centres before the summer timetable went live. The work was divided at the first planning meeting and I was given the payments module, which was the part I knew best. I began by mapping every payment route in the old system, including refunds and part payments, because those had caused faults before. I then wrote the new module over about five weeks, working through card payments first, then vouchers, then the refund path. I wrote unit tests as I went and by the end had just over two hundred of them, and I kept my own notes on each interface as I built it. Halfway through there was some tension in the team about whether we were building too much for the first release. I could see both points of view, but I concentrated on getting my own module finished to the standard I had set myself. I completed it four days ahead of my own estimate and spent the spare time tidying the error messages. The new engine did go live that summer and, as far as I am aware, it has been running reasonably well since.
reason: Own part in a team task described in detail, but no action directed at another person, no step of their own on the tension mentioned and a vague team result, so level 2.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: At the care home there was a falling out between two of the senior carers over who got the weekend shifts, and for a few weeks you could cut the atmosphere with a knife. I did not want to take sides, so I got on with my own residents, did my medication rounds on time and kept my care notes up to date so nothing of mine could be blamed for adding to it. It sorted itself out in the end, I think when the new rota came in, and things went more or less back to normal.
reason: Mentions a disagreement and describes only their own duties, with no step to resolve it and no action towards another person; result vague, so level 2.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: I volunteer at a food bank on Thursdays and before Christmas we had a target of making up three hundred hampers in one evening. There were about a dozen of us. My job was the tinned goods table, so I checked the dates on every tin, sorted them into soup, vegetables and puddings and stacked them in crates of twenty four so they were ready to go into the boxes. Partway through the evening the van bringing the fresh bread was late and some of the others were getting quite stressed about whether we would finish. I just kept going with my tins and by about eight o'clock I had cleared everything that had been donated for my table. I am not sure how many hampers went out in the end, but I think most of them got done and people seemed pleased enough when we locked up.
reason: Own part in a shared task with a difficulty mentioned, but no cooperative action, no step of their own in response and an unstated team result, so level 2.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: I worked weekends at a garden centre and one bank holiday there were only two of us on the outdoor plants section. We both wanted to be out on the floor and neither of us wanted to be stuck on the till in the shed, and by eleven o'clock we were snapping at each other about it in front of customers. I thought that could not go on all day, so at the first quiet moment I told my colleague how long the till queue had got while we were arguing, which was right back to the compost, and I suggested we split the day into two hour turns with me taking the first one on the till. He agreed to that. We stuck to the turns for the rest of the day, the queue never got that long again and we finished the shift on good terms.
reason: Specific example with own role, shares information and offers the first turn, and states a step and its result; no views sought before acting and no change of approach, so level 3 not 4.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: Last year I was one of three teachers given the job of putting on the Year 9 science fair, which had not run for several years. Our shared goal was simple: every pupil in the year group presenting a project to parents on one evening in March. I took responsibility for the timetable and the room plan, one colleague looked after the projects themselves and the third handled letters home and the parents. To keep us joined up I set up a single planning sheet that all three of us could edit and I updated my sections every Friday so the others always knew which rooms and time slots were confirmed. I also asked the colleague leading on projects to check my room plan against the practical work, because she knew far better than I did which experiments needed sinks or power. The main difficulty came ten days before the event, when we found the hall had been double booked for a music exam on the same evening. I walked the building that afternoon, worked out that the library and the two ground floor laboratories could hold the same number of tables between them, redrew the plan and sent the new layout round the next morning. The fair went ahead on the original date across those three rooms, and every one of the planned projects was presented to parents.
reason: Clear role in a shared goal, shares a planning sheet and asks a colleague to check the plan, and responds to the double booking with a stated result; no change of approach after others' views and no concern of another person named, so level 3.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: On a housing site I was with the scaffolding gang and we kept clashing with the bricklayers over the one hoist. Both gangs needed it first thing and it got heated most mornings. One day I went over to their gang, told them which lifts we had booked for that week and what times we would be done, and chalked the times up on the board by the hoist so nobody had to guess. The rows about the hoist stopped after that and both gangs got their materials up each morning for the rest of the week.
reason: Shares information with the other gang and takes a step on the dispute, with the result stated; no views sought, no concern named and no support or credit described, so level 3.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: I was running the grill section at a hotel restaurant when we had a wedding for a hundred and forty booked, and in the week before it the kitchen and the waiting staff were at each other's throats over late plates. My first plan was to rewrite the order of service myself and hand it out. Before I did, I asked two of the waiting staff and the pastry chef what they thought was going wrong. One of the waiters told me his real worry was that guests blamed him to his face when a table's mains came out in two halves, and he had no way of knowing it was coming. That changed my plan. Instead of a new running order I kept the old one and added a call from the pass two minutes before each table was ready, and I asked him to tell me which tables had speeches so we could hold them. On the day our newest commis was falling behind on garnishes, so I took his fish plates onto my section for the main course. At the debrief I made a point of saying the two minute call was the waiter's idea. For the team it meant every table at the wedding got its main course together, and the shouting across the pass that had been going on all week did not happen that night.
reason: Asks for views and changes the plan, names the waiter's concern with specific steps, supports the commis and shares credit, and states what changed; only one side's wants and no lasting practice, so level 4 not 5.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: Our benefits team at the council had to clear a backlog of housing applications before an audit. I had been asked to organise the pile and I was going to split it alphabetically between the five of us, but I asked the others what they thought first. One colleague said she was worried that all the old paper cases would land on her, because she was the only one who knew the previous system. So I changed the split: we sorted by type instead, she showed me how the old cases worked and I took half of them off her. When our manager thanked me for the plan I told him that sorting by type had come from her. We cleared the pile before the audit, and nobody was left carrying the hardest cases alone.
reason: Seeks views before acting and changes the split, names a colleague's concern, shares the work and the credit and states the effect on the team; no two sided disagreement settled and no lasting practice, so level 4.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: So this was at a small software company, about nine of us, and honestly the conflict was partly between me and our tester. I was the developer on a big change to how customer invoices were worked out, and I wanted to ship the whole lot in one go at the end of the month because, well, it was easier for me. She kept pushing back in stand-ups and it was getting a bit frosty. In the end I thought, right, I do not actually know what her problem with it is, so I asked her, and I asked the support lead too since his team would be the ones taking the calls. Turned out her worry was that with everything landing at once she would have two days to test something that touched every customer, and if she missed anything it would be on her. Fair enough, really. So I dropped the one big release. I cut the work into three smaller ones, the first only going to our ten smallest customers, and I sat with her to write the test cases for the first one so she was not starting from nothing. We also had a newer developer who was struggling with the invoice code, so I paired with him two afternoons a week instead of just fixing his bits myself. When the last part went out I said in the team meeting that the staged plan only existed because she had dug her heels in. What it changed was that all three parts went out without us having to pull any of them back, and the stand-ups stopped being awkward.
reason: Asks the tester and support lead before acting and drops the single release, names her concern with specific steps, supports a newer developer and gives credit, and states what changed; no practice the team kept afterwards, so level 4.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: On a residential care unit the night staff and the day staff had fallen out over the morning handover. I was a senior carer on days and had planned to just add ten minutes to it, but I asked both shifts what they wanted before I did anything. The night staff wanted to leave on time, as handover often ran twenty minutes over and one of them was missing her bus. The day staff wanted proper detail on anyone who had had a bad night, because they were finding things out at lunchtime. So I dropped my idea. For the night staff I capped handover at fifteen minutes. For the day staff I drew up a one page sheet, filled in at five each morning, listing only the residents with a change. I filled it in with the newest night carer for her first week. Both shifts agreed at the team meeting to try it for a month, and then to keep it. A year on the unit still uses the sheet, handover finishes on time, and the medication queries we logged after handover fell from about five a week to one.
reason: States what each shift wanted, a step for each and their agreement; the sheet is a practice still in use; result given as a quantity; views were sought first, the plan changed and a colleague was supported, so level 5.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: We had to get fourteen lorries a day out of a furniture warehouse during the January sale, and we were missing about two a day. I was a team leader on the loading side. The pickers and my loaders blamed each other. I thought the answer was more loaders on the late shift, but before asking for that I got three pickers and three loaders together and asked them. The pickers wanted to drop pallets at the nearest door and get back to picking, because they were measured on lines per hour. The loaders wanted each lorry's pallets together, because they were losing twenty minutes a load hunting for them. That was not a staffing problem, so I changed tack. One of my loaders suggested painting a numbered lane for each lorry, and I backed his idea and told the shift manager it was his. For the pickers, I got the lane number printed on the pick sheet so they did not have to think about it. For the loaders, nothing got loaded until its lane was full. I also went on the picks for an hour a day that first week to help them keep their rate up. Both groups signed up to it at the Monday briefing. The lanes are still there now, and for the rest of the sale all fourteen lorries left on time every day.
reason: States what pickers and loaders each wanted, a step for each and that both groups agreed; the lanes are a practice still used; result is a specific quantity; views sought, approach changed, credit shared, so level 5.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer: I help run a Friday community kitchen with about fifteen volunteers. The cooks and the delivery drivers were in a running argument: the cooks wanted to plate up at half past five so the food was fresh, and the drivers wanted to leave by five so the last houses were not eating at eight. I had assumed we should just start cooking earlier, but I asked both groups first, and one driver explained her real concern was two people at the end of her round who went to bed early. So instead I proposed two waves. The cooks kept their half past five plating for the nearby streets, and the far round left at five with meals we had cooked first and packed in insulated boxes. I took over the washing up from one of the cooks so she could do the early batch. Everyone agreed it at the next briefing, we wrote the two waves onto the rota and have used them every Friday since, and all hundred and twenty meals now go out by six.
reason: States what cooks and drivers each wanted, a step for each and that everyone agreed; the two waves are a practice kept every week; result has a quantity and a time; views sought, plan changed, a cook supported, so level 5.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: Problem solving is one of my main strengths. I am analytical and logical, I stay calm under pressure and I am not afraid to think outside the box. I always look at the bigger picture, I pay attention to detail and I never give up until the job is done. In every job I have had, people have come to me when something goes wrong because they know I am solution focused and results driven. Whatever the problem is, I would approach it with a can-do attitude and find a way through.
reason: A list of qualities and general statements with no specific problem and no action described, so level 1.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: The best example I have is from when I worked on the delicatessen counter at a supermarket. For about three weeks the big display chiller kept setting off its alarm in the middle of the afternoon, and nobody could work out why, because every time anyone looked at the dial it was reading the right temperature. The duty manager thought it was the alarm unit itself and had it swapped, which made no difference. Then the store manager decided it was staff leaving the back doors open during restocking and put a sign up, and that made no difference either. In the end head office sent out a refrigeration engineer. He spent most of a morning on it and found that the afternoon sun was coming through a skylight and landing right on the sensor at the top of the cabinet, so the sensor was warming up even though the food was not. He moved the sensor lower down and fitted a little shield over it, and the alarm never went off again after that. I remember it because the cause was so far from what everyone had assumed, and it showed how you can spend weeks looking in the wrong place.
reason: A specific problem, but the engineer and the managers did everything; no action of the candidate's own, so level 1.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: The hardest problem where I worked was the room booking system at the leisure centre. It would let two classes be booked into the same studio at the same time, maybe once or twice a week, and then you had two instructors and two groups turning up at one door. Everybody on reception knew about it and so did the managers. It was really a matter for head office and their supplier, not for front of house staff like me, so there was not a lot to be done at our end. It was still happening when I left. To be honest it showed me how much damage a difficult problem can do when the people at the top are not interested in sorting it out.
reason: Describes a problem that nobody acted on, with no action of their own, so level 1.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: At the cafe where I worked the coffee machine started cutting out in the middle of the morning rush, three or four times in one week. The first thing I thought of was to turn it off at the wall, leave it for a minute and switch it back on, so that is what I did every time it happened. It came back to life each time. I do not know what was actually wrong with it, but after that week I do not remember it being much of a problem, so I suppose that did the trick.
reason: Own action on a specific problem, but it is the first idea tried with no reasoning about the cause, no alternative and no check of the result, so level 2.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: In my role as an administrator for a regional training provider I was responsible for the monthly attendance report that went to our funding body. It was a large workbook that had grown over several years, with a sheet for each of our eleven centres feeding a summary page. In the autumn the totals on the summary page stopped agreeing with the centre sheets. The differences were small, usually between three and nine learners, but they were different every month and the funding body had started to query them, which was uncomfortable for my manager. It was not at all clear where the differences were coming from, and the workbook had been built by someone who had long since left the organisation. I decided that the most reliable course was to start again. Over two weekends I built a completely new workbook from a blank page, set out the eleven centre sheets in a consistent layout, typed the year's figures in again by hand and wrote fresh formulas for the summary. I sent the new version to my manager on the Monday and we have used it ever since. I have not been told of any further queries from the funding body, so I assume the figures are now coming out as they should.
reason: A specific problem and a substantial action of their own, but no information gathered, no cause identified, no alternative weighed and the result assumed, not checked, so level 2.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: I was on the goods-in team at a builders' merchant and one Monday about half of our handheld scanners stopped sending the deliveries through to the stock system. We had lorries waiting in the yard so it needed dealing with quickly. My first thought was the batteries, as they were getting old, so I went round and put a fresh battery in every scanner on the shift, which took me about twenty minutes. A couple of the lads reckoned it was more likely the wireless signal at the back of the shed, but I did not go into that. We carried on booking the deliveries in. I did not hear any more complaints about the scanners that day, though I was moved onto the saw the day after, so I could not tell you for certain whether it lasted.
reason: Acts on the first idea with no reasoning about the cause, sets aside the alternative others raised and does not check whether it worked, so level 2.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I was a senior carer in a residential home and one of our residents, who had been steady on her feet, fell three times in a fortnight. Nobody could see why, as she was fine during the day. I read back through the incident forms and the night logs for the month and I spoke to the two night carers who had found her. Every fall had happened between two and four in the morning, on the way from her bed to her bathroom, and the night carers told me the corridor light outside her room was on a timer that went off at one. So the cause, as I saw it, was that she was getting up for the toilet in the dark. Because of that I asked maintenance to fit a motion light inside her room and I had her bed turned so that she got out on the bathroom side. She did not have another fall in the three months before I moved to a different unit.
reason: Gathers information from logs and night staff, states a cause and links the action to it, and states the result; no causes tested in turn, no options compared and no check described, so level 3.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: I was a supervisor at a discount shop and for three Fridays running one till was short by between twenty and forty pounds. I went through the till rolls for those days and asked the Friday staff to talk me through what they did on a refund. It turned out that a software update had moved the refund button, and one of our newer cashiers had been ringing refunds through as sales and then handing the cash over, which left the till short by exactly the refund amounts. As the cause was the changed screen and not carelessness, I showed him the new layout and had him do three practice refunds with me. The till balanced the following Friday and the Fridays after that.
reason: Checks the till rolls and asks staff, states the cause and why the retraining fits it, and gives the result; no causes tested one at a time and no options compared, so level 3.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I was the only developer supporting a membership website for a professional body, and over about ten days we had a trickle of reports from members who had been signed out seconds after signing in. It was intermittent, it affected perhaps one sign-in in twenty and nobody on the staff could reproduce it, which made it hard to pin down. I started by collecting what we had. I asked the membership team to forward every report with the time it happened, and I pulled the web server logs for the same period and lined the two up. What stood out was that every failed sign-in had been handled by the second of our two web servers, and none by the first. When I looked at that server I found its clock was running nearly six minutes fast. That explained the pattern: a sign-in created on the first server was being treated by the second as not yet valid, so the member was thrown straight back out, while a sign-in that stayed on one server was fine. Because the fault lay in the clock, the fix was to put the clock right, so I corrected the time on the second server and switched on automatic time synchronisation for it. The reports from members stopped the same day and we had none in the months that followed.
reason: Collects reports and logs, states the cause and links the fix to it, and states the result; no possible causes tested one at a time and no options compared, so level 3.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I was a shift supervisor at a warehouse sending out car parts, and our wrong-item returns had roughly doubled in a month with no change in staff or volumes. Rather than guess, I split the job into its three stages, picking, packing and labelling, and checked each on its own. For two days I had every tenth order pulled aside after each stage and compared with the order sheet. The picks and the packed boxes matched every time, but several boxes had another order's label on, always from the bench where two label printers had been moved side by side. I saw two ways to deal with it. One was to move one printer to the far end of the bench, which would take ten minutes but used up the space we kept for oversized parcels. The other was to rebuild the bench so each packer had their own printer, which was the tidier answer but needed new cabling and at least a week. I went for moving the printer, because we were three weeks off our busiest period and I judged losing that space a fair price for a fix that same day. To check it had worked I carried on with the tenth-order checks for a fortnight and found no swapped labels, and the returns figure for the next month was back where it had been.
reason: Breaks the job into stages and checks each, compares two fixes with the trade-off, and says how the result was checked; the choice names no risk or effect on other people and there is no step against recurrence, so level 4.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: I teach maths in a secondary school and homework handed in through our online platform by one of my classes fell from nearly all of them to about half in a few weeks. I tested the likely causes one at a time. First I asked the class whether the tasks were too hard, then I tried the platform on a school laptop, then on my own phone, and it was the phone where it went wrong: photos of written work would not upload. Most of that class only had a phone at home. I weighed up two options. Going back to paper was the simplest, but I would lose the automatic record of who had done what. Keeping the platform and opening the computer room on two lunchtimes kept the record, at the cost of two of my lunch breaks a week. I chose the lunchtimes. To check, I compared the hand-in numbers for the next three weeks with the weeks before, and they were back to nearly the whole class.
reason: Tests likely causes one at a time, compares two options with the trade-off and says how the result was checked; no evidence given for ruling a cause out, no risk or effect on others in the choice and no step against recurrence, so level 4.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I am a site manager for a small house builder, and about four months after handover the owners of one of our flats reported a damp patch under the living room window that kept coming back however often it was wiped down. Damp is awkward because it can come from several directions and the patch itself tells you very little. I listed the three places it could be coming from, which were the heating pipe that runs under that window, condensation from inside the room and rain getting through the outside wall, and I went through them one at a time over a couple of visits instead of opening up the wall straight away. It turned out to be the outside wall, where the mortar joints beside the window frame had not been filled properly. Then there was the question of how to put it right. The quick way was to run a bead of sealant down the joints from a ladder, which would cost very little and take an hour, but sealant in that position only lasts a few years. The other way was to rake out and repoint that section of wall, which meant hiring a tower for two days and cost several times as much, but should last as long as the rest of the brickwork. I chose to repoint, on the grounds that the price difference was small set against the life of the building. I checked it by running a hose over the wall for half an hour once the mortar had cured and then taking moisture meter readings on the inside for the following three weeks, and they stayed dry.
reason: Lists three possible causes and tests them in turn, compares two repairs with the cost and lifespan trade-off and says how the result was checked; no evidence stated for ruling causes out and no risk or people criteria, so level 4.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I was sous chef at a pub kitchen and we started losing salad and dairy from the walk-in fridge, although it read four degrees whenever anyone looked. I put a temperature logger inside for three nights. The obvious suspect was the door seal, but I ruled that out: the seal gripped a sheet of paper all the way round, and the logger showed the fridge only warmed up between two and four in the morning, when nobody was opening the door. Those hours matched the defrost cycle, and I found the defrost timer had gone back to a long default setting after a power cut. I had two options, to turn the thermostat down or to reset the timer. I judged them on food safety for our customers first, then on how long the kitchen would be without the fridge. Turning it down took seconds but risked serving food that had sat warm for two hours a night, so I emptied the fridge for twenty minutes and reset the timer. To confirm it I checked the logger for the next seven nights and it never went above five degrees. To stop it happening again I taped the correct settings inside the door and added a timer check to the opening list for the morning after any power cut.
reason: Rules out the door seal with stated evidence, names the criteria including the risk to customers, says what was checked to confirm the result and adds a step against recurrence, so level 5.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer: I look after the overnight data jobs at an insurance broker, and the job that loads the day's quotes from our supplier began failing about one night in six. I gathered the job logs for two months and tested the likely causes one by one. A network fault was the first idea, and I ruled it out because the monitoring showed no dropped connections on any of the failed nights. A full disk was the second, and I ruled that out because the disk had never been more than sixty per cent used. What the failed nights did share was a supplier file more than twice the usual size, at month end and after bank holidays, and on those nights the load ran past its thirty minute limit and was stopped. I compared two fixes. Raising the limit was a one line change, but the job could then overrun into the morning, when the finance team need the system, and it would hide the files getting bigger. Loading the file in batches was two days of work but kept every run short. My criteria were the risk of holding up the finance team, the effort and how easily I could undo the change, and batching won on the first and third. I confirmed it by re-running the five largest files from the past year, all of which loaded, and by watching the next two month ends. To prevent a repeat I added an alert on file size and put an oversized sample file into our automated tests.
reason: Rules out two named causes with the evidence for each, names criteria including the risk to another team, says what was checked to confirm the fix and adds steps against recurrence, so level 5.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer: I am a volunteer driver for a community minibus and the wheelchair lift started sticking halfway up on cold mornings. Everyone said it was the battery. I ruled that out, because the meter showed 12.6 volts and the lift still stuck with the engine running. The fluid in the lift pump was the next thing I checked, and it was low and as thick as treacle in the cold. I could top it up with the same fluid or have it drained and refilled with a winter grade. What mattered to me was the risk of a passenger being stuck in mid air, and after that how long the bus would be off the road for the people who rely on it. Topping up was quicker but left that risk, so I booked the refill and arranged a taxi for the Tuesday run. To confirm it I ran the lift ten times each morning for a week of frosts and it did not stick once. Then I added a fluid check to the autumn service sheet so it does not catch us out again.
reason: Rules out the battery with stated evidence, names criteria including the risk to passengers and the effect on users, says what was checked to confirm the result and adds a step against recurrence, so level 5.
